triage.name: Drug allergy
triage.reason: Broad category rather than a single diagnosis; overlaps with specific reactions (penicillin allergy, serum sickness) and is better taught as those entities.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'tryptase' (not in the reference table)
exam: term 'Focal neurological deficit' not found in SNOMED CT

age.peak: any age; often first recognized in adulthood after new drug exposure

demographics: Can occur at any age; many first reactions are recognized in adulthood when a new drug is started
Reported penicillin allergy is more common in women
Reactions are more frequent in people with frequent antibiotic or healthcare exposure

risk_factors.text: Prior reaction to the same drug or a chemically related drug
Repeated or prolonged exposure to the drug
Concurrent use of drugs that cause histamine release or interact with mast cells

family_history: Drug allergy in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I broke out in a rash after starting a new medicine
My face and lips are swelling
I feel like I can't breathe

hpi.onset: Minutes to hours after a dose for immediate reactions; days to weeks after starting the drug for delayed reactions
hpi.duration: Minutes to days for acute reactions; may persist or recur with continued exposure
hpi.progression: Immediate reactions peak within an hour; delayed reactions evolve over days and may worsen with each dose
hpi.location: Generalized skin, or localized to face, lips, tongue, throat, or injection site
hpi.quality: Itchy raised welts, flushing, or a spreading red rash; swelling of soft tissues; wheezing or throat tightness in severe cases
hpi.severity: Mild itching and rash to life-threatening breathing difficulty and low blood pressure
hpi.timing: Temporally related to drug administration; immediate reactions within 1 hour, delayed reactions after 6 hours to days

associated_symptoms.text: Itchy raised welts on the skin
Flushing or redness of the skin
Swelling of the face, lips, or tongue

pertinent_negatives: No new food, insect sting, or latex exposure
No personal or family history of recurrent angioedema without a trigger
No symptoms before the suspected drug was started
No isolated gastrointestinal symptoms without skin or respiratory involvement

positives.text: Swelling of the face or lips

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may present with irritability, feeding difficulty, and a rash that is harder to characterize; delayed reactions such as maculopapular exanthems are common.
May present with less prominent skin findings and more systemic symptoms; polypharmacy increases risk and makes attribution difficult.
Physiologic changes can alter drug metabolism and immune response; presentation is similar but management must consider fetal safety.
May have blunted or atypical skin findings and more severe systemic reactions; drug allergy can be confused with infection or graft-versus-host disease.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; itching and rash are the main complaint
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, scratching, anxious but not toxic-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, restless or anxious, flushed, may be wheezing or hoarse
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or cyanotic, diaphoretic, confused or lethargic, in respiratory distress

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the trunk, limbs, and pressure areas
findings.finding: Raised, blanching, erythematous wheals of varying size with surrounding flare

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, neck, and upper trunk
findings.finding: Diffuse erythema and warmth of the skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk and extremities for a spreading rash
findings.finding: Confluent maculopapular erythematous rash, often starting on the trunk

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the lips, periorbital tissue, tongue, and oral cavity
findings.finding: Non-pitting, non-tender swelling of the lips, eyelids, tongue, or oral soft tissue

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs during quiet and forced expiration
Auscultate over the larynx and trachea while the patient breathes quietly
findings.finding: High-pitched inspiratory sound over the upper airway

findings.maneuver: Listen to the patient's voice and ask about voice change
findings.finding: Hoarse or muffled voice suggesting laryngeal edema

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms and repeat after standing if the patient can tolerate it
findings.finding: Low systolic blood pressure with or without orthostatic drop

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and count the rate
Inspect the conjunctivae and periorbital area
findings.finding: Red, injected conjunctivae with or without tearing

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate
findings.finding: Painful ulceration or erosion of the oral mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for blistering, sheet-like detachment, or peeling, and check for a positive Nikolsky sign
findings.finding: Peeling or sloughing of the skin, especially at pressure points or mucosal junctions
Fine inspiratory crackles at the bases

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 30–45 degrees
Perform a brief neurologic screen including strength, sensation, and cranial nerves
findings.finding: Asymmetric weakness, sensory loss, or cranial nerve abnormality

labs.caveat: Eosinophilia supports a drug reaction but is often absent in acute IgE-mediated reactions; it is more typical of delayed reactions such as DRESS.
Leukocytosis is nonspecific and can reflect infection or systemic inflammation rather than the drug reaction itself.
Thrombocytopenia suggests a drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia or a systemic reaction such as DRESS.
Transaminitis raises concern for drug-induced liver injury or DRESS rather than a simple urticarial reaction.
Rising creatinine suggests a systemic reaction with renal involvement, such as acute interstitial nephritis or DRESS.
Nonspecific; helps gauge systemic inflammation in delayed or severe reactions.

findings.finding: Sinus rhythm; may show ectopy in severe reactions
Diffuse ST depression or nonspecific ST-T changes with hypotension or hypoperfusion
QT prolongation from concomitant QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte disturbance

findings.text: Usually normal; no infiltrate or edema in an uncomplicated drug reaction
Hyperinflation or air trapping when bronchospasm is prominent
Patchy infiltrates or pulmonary edema in severe systemic reactions

initial.why: Looks for eosinophilia, leukocytosis, or cytopenias that suggest a systemic drug reaction
Assesses hepatic and renal involvement in delayed or severe reactions
Evaluates for an alternative cause of wheeze or dyspnea
initial.only_if: respiratory symptoms are prominent or anaphylaxis is suspected

confirmatory.why: Confirms IgE-mediated allergy to a specific drug, most often a beta-lactam, when the history is unclear
confirmatory.only_if: the culprit drug is known and the patient is stable enough for testing

confirmatory.why: Supports an IgE-mediated mechanism for selected drugs such as penicillins
confirmatory.only_if: skin testing is unavailable or contraindicated

confirmatory.why: Definitive test when skin and serologic testing are negative or unavailable
confirmatory.only_if: performed under supervision with resuscitation available

supporting.why: Supports mast cell activation when drawn soon after a suspected anaphylactic reaction
May identify the culprit in delayed cutaneous reactions such as maculopapular exanthem or DRESS

not_indicated.why: No role in drug allergy; would only mislead toward thromboembolic disease
Does not distinguish a drug reaction from infection and is not part of the workup
Rarely changes management; reserve for suspected complications or an alternative diagnosis

decision_points: Stop the suspected drug immediately and treat anaphylaxis with epinephrine before any testing
Do not perform skin testing or challenge during an acute severe reaction or within weeks of anaphylaxis
Distinguish immediate IgE-mediated reactions from delayed T-cell reactions, since the testing strategy differs
Consider drug-induced liver injury, DRESS, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome when fever, transaminitis, cytopenias, or mucosal involvement are present

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Drug exposure followed by urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, and hypotension is the classic picture of anaphylaxis, which is the most severe form of an immediate drug allergy.
differential.trigger: Hypotension, airway swelling, or respiratory distress after a drug dose

history: Symptoms begin within minutes of the dose
Rapid progression over minutes to an hour
Sense of impending doom or throat closing
exam: Stridor or hoarseness from laryngeal edema
labs: Elevated serum tryptase drawn within a few hours of onset
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or shows hyperinflation

differential.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
differential.why_considered: A delayed drug reaction that begins with fever and a rash and can be mistaken for a benign morbilliform drug eruption early on.
differential.trigger: Painful skin, mucosal erosions, or skin peeling after starting a new drug

history: Onset 1 to 3 weeks after starting the culprit drug
Painful skin and mucosal sores
Fever and malaise before the rash
exam: Mucosal erosions of the mouth, eyes, or genitals
Sheet-like skin detachment or a positive Nikolsky sign
Widespread dusky macules coalescing into blisters
labs: Cytopenias and elevated transaminases may be present

differential.name: DRESS syndrome
differential.why_considered: A delayed drug hypersensitivity that presents with fever, rash, and facial edema and is often mistaken for a simple drug rash or a viral exanthem.
differential.trigger: Fever, facial swelling, and a widespread rash 2 to 8 weeks after starting a drug

history: Fever and malaise preceding the rash
Facial swelling
Recent start of an anticonvulsant, sulfonamide, or allopurinol
exam: Widespread morbilliform rash with facial edema
No mucosal blistering or skin detachment

differential.name: Viral exanthem
differential.why_considered: A morbilliform rash with fever in a patient taking a new medication can be caused by a viral infection rather than the drug.

history: Preceding or concurrent viral symptoms such as cough, coryza, or sore throat
Sick contacts
Rash appears during or after the febrile illness rather than after a new drug
exam: Diffuse maculopapular rash without urticaria or angioedema

differential.name: Chronic spontaneous urticaria
differential.why_considered: Recurrent hives and itching can be attributed to a drug when no external trigger is actually responsible.

history: Recurrent wheals for more than 6 weeks
No clear temporal relationship to any drug dose
Symptoms may be worse at night or with pressure
exam: Urticaria without angioedema or systemic symptoms

differential.name: Hereditary angioedema
differential.why_considered: Recurrent swelling of the face, lips, or extremities can be mistaken for drug-induced angioedema.

history: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria since childhood or adolescence
Family history of similar swelling
Abdominal pain attacks
labs: Low C4 and C1 inhibitor levels or function

differential.name: Serum sickness
differential.why_considered: Fever, rash, and joint pain appearing 1 to 2 weeks after a drug or biologic can mimic a delayed drug allergy.

history: Exposure to a biologic or a drug 1 to 2 weeks earlier
Fever, arthralgias, and malaise
Symptoms resolve after stopping the drug
labs: Normal eosinophil count or mild elevation

differential.name: Drug-induced thrombocytopenia
differential.why_considered: A drug reaction that presents with petechiae or bruising rather than urticaria, and can be confused with a cutaneous drug eruption.

history: Petechiae or easy bruising after starting a new drug
No itching or hives
Recent exposure to heparin, quinine, or sulfonamides

severity.mild: Localized itching, a few urticarial wheals, or a mild maculopapular rash without systemic symptoms; vital signs normal.
severity.moderate: Widespread urticaria or rash with pruritus, mild angioedema of the lips or eyelids, or mild wheezing; vital signs stable but uncomfortable.
severity.severe: Marked angioedema, stridor, bronchospasm, hypotension, or a systemic delayed reaction with fever, facial edema, and organ involvement.
severity.critical: Anaphylaxis with shock, airway compromise, or respiratory failure; or a severe cutaneous reaction with skin detachment and mucosal involvement.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or syncope after a drug dose

red_flags.meaning: Bronchospasm from anaphylaxis; needs immediate treatment
Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis; stop the drug and admit

red_flags.finding: Fever, facial edema, and eosinophilia weeks after starting a drug
red_flags.meaning: DRESS syndrome; risk of organ failure
Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia; risk of bleeding

complications.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis

special_populations.differences: Delayed maculopapular exanthems are common and often benign; immediate reactions are less frequent than in adults. Careful history is needed to avoid unnecessary avoidance of antibiotics.
Polypharmacy makes attribution difficult; skin findings may be less prominent and systemic reactions more severe. Renal and hepatic impairment increase the risk of drug accumulation.
Presentation is similar, but management must consider fetal safety; epinephrine is still first-line for anaphylaxis. Penicillin allergy testing can be performed safely in pregnancy when indicated.
Skin findings may be blunted or atypical, and drug reactions can be confused with infection or graft-versus-host disease. A lower threshold for biopsy and drug discontinuation is warranted.

key_questions.question: Which medicine do you think caused this, and when did you take it relative to your symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: A specific culprit drug with a clear temporal relationship: within 1 hour for immediate reactions, 6 hours to days for delayed reactions

key_questions.question: How soon after the dose did the symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: Minutes to 1 hour suggests IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity; days to weeks suggests a delayed T-cell reaction

key_questions.question: What exactly happened — what did the reaction look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Hives, flushing, swelling, wheezing, or a spreading rash; helps classify the reaction type

key_questions.question: Was there any trouble breathing, throat tightness, or feeling faint?
key_questions.looking_for: Airway or circulatory involvement indicating anaphylaxis

key_questions.question: Have you taken this drug or a similar one since, and what happened?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrence with re-exposure supports true allergy; tolerance on re-exposure argues against it

key_questions.question: How was the reaction treated, and how long did it take to resolve?
key_questions.looking_for: Response to antihistamines or epinephrine; rapid resolution after stopping the drug

key_questions.question: Are you taking any other medicines, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: All current drugs and the timing of any recent additions, to identify the culprit and interacting agents

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction to a medicine before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior drug reactions and any cross-reactive agents

key_questions.question: Do you have any other allergies, such as food, latex, or insect stings?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopy or other triggers that may explain the symptoms

key_questions.question: Do you have asthma or any mast cell disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that increase the risk and severity of reactions

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a drug allergy or recurrent swelling without hives?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of drug allergy or hereditary angioedema

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, facial swelling, or feeling generally unwell since starting the drug?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic features suggesting DRESS or another severe delayed reaction

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any sores in your mouth, eyes, or genitals, or any skin peeling?
key_questions.looking_for: Mucosal involvement or skin detachment suggesting Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis

key_questions.question: Any bruising or tiny red spots on the skin?

reasoning_points: A specific drug was started or taken shortly before the symptoms began
The timing fits an immediate (minutes to 1 hour) or delayed (days to weeks) hypersensitivity reaction
Symptoms include typical allergic features such as urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema, wheezing, or hypotension
Symptoms improve or resolve after stopping the suspected drug
Alternative causes such as infection, viral exanthem, or chronic urticaria are considered and excluded
Red flags for anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous reactions are specifically assessed

easy: Clear temporal relationship between a new drug and urticaria or angioedema
Itching and raised wheals on exam
Symptoms resolve after stopping the drug
medium: Delayed maculopapular rash days after starting an antibiotic
Multiple new medications make the culprit uncertain
Mild wheezing or facial swelling without hypotension
Reaction reported in the past but details are vague
hard: Reaction occurs during a serious infection, making attribution difficult
Fever, facial edema, and eosinophilia suggesting DRESS rather than a simple rash
Mucosal erosions or skin peeling suggesting Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Patient presents with isolated hypotension or respiratory distress and cannot give a history
Symptoms overlap with chronic spontaneous urticaria or hereditary angioedema
